chief_complaint: difficulty swallowing both food and liquids for 9 months
hpi_details: 9-month worsening dysphagia equally affecting solid food and liquids from the onset. Experiences sensation of food sticking in the lower chest, frequent regurgitation of bland, undigested food at night, and retrosternal chest tightness. Lost 4kg over 6 months due to fear of eating. Denies heartburn or acid taste.
ideas: thinks her throat muscles have stopped working properly
concerns: afraid she might choke to death while sleeping due to regurgitation
expectations: wants a procedure to open up her esophagus so she can drink fluids normally
social_hx: non-smoker, drinks wine socially, teacher, sleeps propped up on three pillows

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Achalasia is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Referral for high-resolution manometry and diagnostic gastroscopy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: difficulty swallowing both food and liquids for 9 months

Key HPI features: 9-month worsening dysphagia equally affecting solid food and liquids from the onset. Experiences sensation of food sticking in the lower chest, frequent regurgitation of bland, undigested food at night, and retrosternal chest tightness. Lost 4kg over 6 months due to fear of eating. Denies heartburn or acid taste.

Objective/Exam findings: General exam for nutrition status. OGD (gastroscopy) to exclude mechanical obstruction or pseudoachalasia (malignancy at gastro-oesophageal junction). High-resolution oesophageal manometry (gold standard showing aperistalsis and failure of LES relaxation). Barium swallow ('bird-beak' appearance).
Relevant background/PMH: hypothyroidism, mild allergic rhinitis
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Achalasia.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Gastric cardia adenocarcinoma (pseudoachalasia) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Choking or aspiration risk from nighttime regurgitation.
management_principles: Referral for high-resolution manometry and diagnostic gastroscopy
Discuss therapeutic options: pneumatic dilation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy, or Per-Oral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM)
Advise upright posture for 2 hours after meals and sleeping with head elevated
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 48F presents with 9-month progressive dysphagia to solids AND liquids from onset, regurgitation of undigested food, retrosternal fullness, and 4kg weight loss.
reference_soap.objective: General exam for nutrition status. OGD (gastroscopy) to exclude mechanical obstruction or pseudoachalasia (malignancy at gastro-oesophageal junction). High-resolution oesophageal manometry (gold standard showing aperistalsis and failure of LES relaxation). Barium swallow ('bird-beak' appearance).
reference_soap.assessment: Achalasia cardiae. DDx: pseudoachalasia secondary to gastric cardia adenocarcinoma, diffuse oesophageal spasm, peptic stricture, eosinophilic oesophagitis.
reference_soap.plan: Referral for high-resolution manometry and diagnostic gastroscopy. Discuss therapeutic options: pneumatic dilation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy, or Per-Oral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM). Advise upright posture for 2 hours after meals and sleeping with head elevated.

learning_objectives: Differentiate motility dysphagia (solids and liquids simultaneously) from mechanical stricture (solids progressing to liquids)
Identify nocturnal regurgitation and aspiration risk factors in esophageal outflow obstruction
Outline the diagnostic step-up approach: endoscopy, barium contrast, and manometry
Discuss definitive interventions for lower esophageal sphincter hypertonicity clearly

teaching.one_liner: The lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax and the oesophagus loses its normal squeezing motion, so both solids and liquids get stuck and come back up.
red_flags: Choking or aspiration risk from nighttime regurgitation

must_ask.say: Does it feel like both solid food and liquids get stuck, right from the start?
Do you ever bring up food that looks undigested, especially at night?
Where do you feel the tightness — is it behind your breastbone?

must_ask.objective: Weight loss and fear of eating
must_ask.say: Have you lost weight because you're avoiding food out of fear of it sticking?
Why do you sleep propped up on pillows — is it to stop the regurgitation?
Do you get any heartburn or acid taste, or is it just the food sticking?
